subject: Cognitive Science
title: Nudge Theory
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Nudge Theory.

hook.text: Countries that make organ donation opt-out instead of opt-in see donation rates jump from 15% to over 90%.

buildup.text: Thaler and Sunstein call this a 'nudge': redesigning the choice environment without removing any options.

discovery.text: Defaults are enormously powerful because people tend to stick with whatever is pre-selected.

twist.text: Nudges are controversial. Critics call it paternalism—manipulating choices while pretending people are free.

climax.text: The UK created a 'Nudge Unit' inside government. Its interventions have saved billions in tax collection alone.

punchline.text: Change the default, change the decision.

quiz.question: What is a 'nudge' in decision science?
options: Redesigning choice environments without removing options

details.summary: Thaler and Sunstein proposed that small changes in how choices are presented, called nudges, can steer behavior without limiting freedom. Default organ donation enrollment, smaller plates for portions, and automatic savings plans are nudges that exploit predictable biases for beneficial outcomes.
details.whyItMatters: Nudge theory enables policymakers to improve decisions by redesigning choice architecture rather than mandating behavior. It bridges behavioral science and public policy.
takeaways: Small presentation changes steer decisions significantly
Defaults are the most powerful nudge tool
Nudges preserve freedom of choice while improving outcomes

faq.question: What makes defaults such powerful nudges?
faq.answer: Most people stick with the default option because switching requires effort and attention. Opt-out organ donation, where you are enrolled unless you decline, produces donation rates above 90 percent. Opt-in systems produce rates below 20 percent. The same choice, radically different outcomes.

faq.question: Are nudges ethical or manipulative?
faq.answer: Critics argue nudges are paternalistic and bypass rational deliberation. Defenders say people face nudges everywhere since no choice is presented neutrally.
